1. The rate of sulphation of a sulphatable compound by the isolated perfused guinea pig liver depends upon the concentration of SO42- in the perfusate; and that the sulphuryl enzyme is the rate-limiting step.

the inhibition by chlorate, presumably through the inhibition of ATP-sulphurlyase, may be a useful tool to study the sulphation of endogenous and foreign compounds when the activity of this enzyme is rate-limiting, but that it does not inhibit the sulphation of compounds whose synthesis of PAPS, the immediate precursor of the sulphate, is rate-limiting.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for the isolation and identification of sulphated metabolites of steroid hormones.
the development of a model system to investigate the metabolism of oestrone sulphate and oestrone glucuronide in the isolated perfusion system.
the study of the mechanisms involved in the regulation of the synthesis of the active sulphur donor, PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phospho-sulphate).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the sulphation reactions in rat liver, chlorates are not inhibitors of the synthesis of PAP or of the transfer of the sulphate group to the phenol, but are inhibitors of the synthesis, in liver, of sulphate from inorganic sulphate.
chlorate is not an effective inhibitor of PAPS synthesis by the perfused guinea-pig liver.
chlorate is not an inhibitor of the sulphurylation of PAPS, but that it is an inhibitor of the subsequent transfer of sulphate to the sulphate acceptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sulphation of PEG-200 by the isolated guinea pig liver, and of oestrone by the rat liver microsomal preparation, are both dependent on ATP-sulphonylase.
chlorate inhibits the sulphation of PEG200 by rat liver microsomal preparations, but not by rat liver homogenates.
chlorate is not only an inhibitor of ATP-sulphate synthetase but also an inhibitor of sulphation of polyethylene glycol 200 in guinea pig liver perfusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chlorate is not toxic to the liver in a short term perfusion.
the rate of synthesis of the sulphur donor PAPS can be controlled by the use of chlorate in the perfusate, and that the rate of the sulphation reaction is independent of the availability of PAPS.
chlorate is a useful inhibitor of the sulphation reaction when the synthesis of PAPs is rate-limiting.
